name: zapoteco de Comaltepec, Choapan
confidence_why: Lyman & Lyman 1977 and Lyman Boulden 2010 agree that Comaltepec Choapan Zapotec stresses the penultimate syllable of the root unless a syllable with a two-vowel or vowel-plus-nasal nucleus draws the stress, with a few lexical exceptions such as belo 'star' against beló 'cave', and Morales Camacho 2021 finds the same weight-sensitive trochaic pattern in the neighbouring Sochiapan variety; the sources differ only in how strongly the 1977 paper plays up the exceptions as making stress unpredictable, and both Comaltepec descriptions come from the same SIL fieldwork lineage.

catalog_quote: Normalmente en el ZC, la penúltima sílaba de la raíz es la sílaba tónica. En los ejemplos que siguen, las sílabas tónicas están marcadas con un acento gráfico sobre una de sus vocales. béco' perro / chíta hueso, huevo / žítu gato / gúba escoba. Sin embargo, si la raíz tiene una sílaba con dos vocales, o una vocal con una nasal, esa sílaba será la sílaba tónica y la primera vocal de esa sílaba será la vocal acentuada. bžu'láo mono, chango / beláo importante / bá'ohua máscara / gá'acaga un poco / badán bonito / ubín hambre / bezén rocío / bezún sonajero. Si la raíz tiene una sílaba que consiste en la combinación de i o u más otra vocal, esa sílaba será la sílaba tónica y la vocal que sigue a i o u será la vocal acentuada. Mariá María / bëduá chorro de agua / ruéro estamos haciendo / rióro estamos yendo / biú' luna, mes / xcuídi' niño. En el caso de palabras compuestas, es la segunda raíz de la palabra la que tiene la sílaba tónica de acuerdo con las reglas ya mencionadas. ... rbialáoro Estamos adelantando. / rezi'lá'dyi'ro Estamos descansando. / xuzixtá'oro nuestros antepasados. En el uso popular se escribe el acento gráfico en la palabra solamente cuando la sílaba tónica queda fuera de las reglas de acentuación y existe otra palabra con la que se puede confundir. Es decir, cuando la sílaba tónica no es la penúltima como en beló cueva y guibá cielo y existen otras palabras como belo estrella y guiba fierro, metal.

new_statements.translation: Normally in Comaltepec Zapotec (ZC), the penultimate syllable of the root is the stressed syllable. [...] However, if the root has a syllable with two vowels, or a vowel plus a nasal, that syllable will be the stressed syllable, and the first vowel of that syllable will be the accented vowel. [...] If the root has a syllable consisting of i or u plus another vowel, that syllable will be the stressed syllable, and the vowel following i or u will be the accented vowel. [...] In compound words it is the second root of the word that carries the stressed syllable, according to the rules already given.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root by default, but a heavy root syllable (two vowels, i.e. a complex/diphthongal nucleus, or vowel + nasal) attracts the stress wherever it is; in compounds the second root is stressed by the same rules. Lyman & Lyman 1977: 149 give the same generalisation for the same variety ('Stress most often occurs on a syllable having a complex nucleus unless the syllables are all of equal length, in which case stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable') but add that exceptions make stress unpredictable; stressed syllables are longer. The language also has three register tones with extensive sandhi (Lyman Boulden 2010: 11-12; Lyman & Lyman 1977: 141, 152-159).
new_statements.exceptions: Lyman Boulden 2010: 10: stress is written only 'cuando la sílaba tónica queda fuera de las reglas de acentuación y existe otra palabra con la que se puede confundir', e.g. beló 'cueva' vs belo 'estrella', guibá 'cielo' vs guiba 'fierro' (final stress off-rule). Lyman & Lyman 1977: 149: 'There are, however, a number of exceptions. It is these exceptions that make it impossible to predict stress even if long vowels are posited', e.g. ultimate stress in ro¹la³láo³-bi'¹ 'he/she is going ahead' and rio³nie³-da'³ 'I understand' although both syllables have complex nuclei; minimal pair bé²lo² 'star' vs be²ló² 'cave'. Lyman Boulden 2010: 78-79: the completive prefix gu- keeps its g only when it is the stressed syllable (gúlero) and loses it when unstressed (unáro).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/grammatical word in citation form (the 1977 paper: phonological word boundaries 'determined on the basis of words in isolation, in which case they coincide with the boundaries of the grammatical word'). Lyman & Lyman 1977 sec. 4 (pp. 150-151) additionally describe a phrase-level stress/length peak (non-amazement vs amazement phrases) whose placement is 'not clearly understood'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Zapotec of San Juan Comaltepec, distrito de Choapan, Oaxaca (Lyman & Lyman 1977 fn. 1 p. 160: data from Comaltepec, informants Concepción Gonzales and Máximo Jiménez; Lyman Boulden 2010 title and SIL record 52338), which SIL and Glottolog treat as Choapan Zapotec [zpc] = choa1237; the 1977 paper defines the dialect area as Comaltepec (south) to Arenal Grande (north). Hernández Andrade 2011 covers two Zapotec varieties in San Juan Jaltepec (Yaveo, Choapan district), also under choa1237, and is silent on stress.

new_statements.quote: Stress most often occurs on a syllable having a complex nucleus unless the syllables are all of equal length, in which case stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable. There are, however, a number of exceptions. It is these exceptions that make it impossible to predict stress even if long vowels are posited. For example, in [ro¹la³láo³-biʔ¹] he/she (informal) is going ahead and [rio³nie³-daʔ³] I understand, the stress occurs on the ultimate rather than penultimate syllable, even though both syllables have complex nuclei. In cases such as bé²lo² star and be²ló² cave, the stressed syllable is longer in each case because all stressed syllables are longer than unstressed syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the phonological word (a 'stress unit' whose nucleus coincides with the grammatical stem, p. 148), stress most often falls on the syllable with a complex nucleus (two or three vowel segments); when all syllables are of equal length it usually falls on the penultimate syllable. Stress placement is otherwise lexical: bisyllabic stems are penult- or final-stressed, tri- and quadrisyllabic stems antepenult-, penult- or final-stressed (p. 148 chart), and the authors say the exceptions make stress unpredictable even if vowel length were posited. Stressed syllables are longer than unstressed ones (length is the correlate of stress). Three register tones, extensive tone sandhi.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress is mentioned. Sec. 4 (pp. 150-151) describes phrase stress: the peak of a phonological phrase (1-5 P words) carries stress and length 'more prominent than that of the P word itself'; its placement across the words of the phrase is 'not clearly understood at present'.
new_statements.exceptions: Yes: 'a number of exceptions' that make stress unpredictable, e.g. final stress in stems where both syllables have complex nuclei (he/she is going ahead; I understand); minimal pair bé²lo² 'star' vs be²ló² 'cave' distinguished by stress position; stress subtypes (penult/ultimate; antepenult/penult/ultimate) listed as lexical types of P word on p. 148.
new_statements.identity_note: The volume covers several Otomanguean languages; only the Lyman & Lyman chapter (pp. 137-161, confirmed from the table of contents, p. v) is about this language. Footnote 1 (p. 160): the Choapan dialect area runs from Comaltepec in the south to Arenal Grande in the north; data were collected at Comaltepec from two Comaltepec speakers (Concepción Gonzales, 33, and Máximo Jiménez, 28). This is the same Comaltepec variety as the catalog item and as Lyman Boulden 2010.

One minor stress-related passage in the same chapter that the compiler report does not mention: sec. 2.1, p. 142 (p. 150; the scanned textof the chapter file), rule (1): 'The first rule deals only with laryngeal vowels and specifies the placement of stress and glottal stop' -- a laryngeal vowel is realized as a stressed vowel plus glottal stop when another vowel follows, otherwise as stressed vowel + glottal stop + echo vowel; i.e. within a laryngeal complex nucleus the stress sits on its first vowel, which matches the 2010 grammar's 'la primera vocal de esa sílaba será la vocal acentuada'.…

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among the sources. Lyman & Lyman 1977 (p. 149) and Lyman Boulden 2010 (sec. 2.5, pp. 9-10, already in existing_statements) give the same picture for the Comaltepec variety: penultimate syllable of the stem by default, a syllable with a complex (two-vowel) nucleus attracts stress, and lexical exceptions marked by stress-position minimal pairs (the same pair, bé²lo² 'star' vs be²ló² 'cave' = belo/beló, appears in both). They differ only in emphasis: the 1977 paper says the exceptions make stress 'impossible to predict even if long vowels are posited', while the 2010 grammar frames penult-of-root as the norm ('normalmente') and writes an accent only on off-rule words that form minimal pairs. The 2010 grammar's clause that a vowel+nasal syllable also attracts stress has no counterpart in the 1977 paper. The earlier entry for Morales Camacho 2021 (Santiago Sochiapan variety, moraic trochee with stress-to-weight lengthening, stem-initial stress in simple roots; not among the works in this task) is a different Choapan-area variety and a different analysis (stress conditions length rather than the reverse), but not a contradiction of the Comaltepec placement.

sources.note: Open-access, instrumentally supported description of stress in a Choapan (choa1237) variety: stressed syllable = root-initial (penult in bisyllabic roots), must be bimoraic (moraic trochee; lengthening non-contrastive, stress-to-weight), primary stress on the second trochee of compounds (duration measured over 40 items), stress culminative, contour tones only on stressed syllables, TBU = mora. Gives the catalog a second, modern, phonetically grounded statement for the language and a foot-based analysis to set beside Lyman Boulden's heavy-syllable rule. Already downloaded: (+.xml).
